sequence.vyakhya: कुम्भं करोतीति कुम्भकारः। कर्मणि उपपदे कृधातोः अण्प्रत्ययः। उपपदं कर्म च समस्यते एकपदे।
sequence.vyakhya_en: When an object (कर्मन्) stands as उपपद beside a root, the root takes अण् to form an agent-noun. Here कुम्भ "pot" joins कृ "make" and the affix अण् gives कुम्भकारः "pot-maker." The object does not stay a separate accusative word; it merges into a single तत्पुरुष compound with the agent-noun.

sequence.vyakhya: गां ददातीति गोदः। आकारान्तात् दाधातोः अनुपसर्गात् कर्मण्युपपदे कप्रत्ययः। एवं धनदः जलदश्च।
sequence.vyakhya_en: A root ending in long आ, with no उपसर्ग before it and an object standing as उपपद, takes क instead of अण्. Thus गो "cow" + दा "give" + क yields गोदः "cow-giver." The same pattern gives धनदः "wealth-giver" and जलदः "water-giver" (the cloud). The object गो merges with the agent-noun into one तत्पुरुष compound.

sequence.translation: The delighting son gladdens his mother.
sequence.teaches: ल्यु (→ अन) forms an agent-noun from नन्दि-group roots.

notes.role: नन्दिग्रहिपचादिभ्यो ल्युणिन्यचः → नन्द् + ल्यु (अन) → नन्दनः

notes.en: agent-noun in अन from the नन्दि-group

quiz.q: Which form is मातृ · द्वितीया · एकवचन?

sequence.vyakhya: नन्दतीति नन्दनः। नन्दिग्रहिपचादिगणे नन्दिधातोः ल्युप्रत्ययः, यस्य अनादेशः।
sequence.vyakhya_en: Roots of the नन्दि-group take ल्यु, and ल्यु is replaced by अन, giving agent-nouns like नन्दनः "the delighting one, the son." Unlike अण् and क above, this ल्यु-formation needs no उपपद object to attach; the affix alone names the doer. The same rule routes ग्रहि-roots to णिनि and पच्-group roots to अच्.

sequence.translation: The king was wealthy and brave. He had a messenger bring wealth, and gave it to the brahmins. Thus he became a great giver. All sang of his bravery. The king, having heard that, laughed, but felt no pride.

(शूरत्वम्, "bravery"), one possessive (धनवान्), one gerund (श्रुत्वा) — four
parts of speech in five clauses.

sequence.vyakhya: एकस्मिन्नेव आख्याने णिच्, तृच्, त्व, मतुप्, क्त्वा — चत्वारः शब्दप्रकाराः।
sequence.vyakhya_en:
Four ways of building a word, in one short scene. आनाययत् is a **causative**:
नी "lead" plus णिच् becomes आनाय् "cause to bring," and the one who would have
been the agent — दूतम् — drops to the accusative (1.4.52), because the king is
now the one causing. दाता is an **agent-noun**, दा "give" plus तृच्, "the
giver." शूरत्वम् is an **abstract**, शूर "brave" plus त्व, "bravery" — a quality
named as a thing. धनवान् is a **possessive**, धन plus मतुप्, "wealth-having."
And श्रुत्वा is a **gerund**: श्रु plus क्त्वा, indeclinable, "having heard."
The nouns around them — दूतम्, धनम्, ब्राह्मणेभ्यः, गर्वम् — sit in cases the
reader has long since met; only the five built words are new.

sequence.sentence: सुतप्तम् अपि पानीयं शमयत्य् एव पावकम्।
sequence.translation: Even well-heated water puts out fire.
sequence.teaches: the first line of Pañcatantra — a complete maxim, with the particle अपि

notes.role: अतोऽम् — the neuter अ-stem takes अम् in प्रथमा and द्वितीया → सुतप्तम्

notes.en: adjective qualifying पानीयम् (agrees with it — neuter, प्रथमा)

notes.role: स्वतन्त्रः कर्ता → पानीय (water) is the agent
अतोऽम् — neuter a-stem प्रथमा → पानीयम् (→ पानीयं, anusvāra before श)
वर्तमाने लट् → present
कर्तुरीप्सिततमं कर्म → पावक (fire) is the कर्मन्
कर्मणि द्वितीया → पावकम्

sequence.vyakhya: पानीयं कर्तृ, पावकम् कर्म, शमयति क्रिया। अपि-शब्देन विरोधः सूच्यते।
sequence.vyakhya_en: A complete Pañcatantra maxim, and it parses cleanly: पानीयं (water, कर्तृ/प्रथमा) शमयति (extinguishes) पावकम् (fire, कर्मन्/द्वितीया). The particle अपि ("even") + सुतप्तम् ("well-heated") carry the twist — even water that has itself been heated still quells fire. Real text, real rhetoric, grammar you hold.

sequence.sentence: गुरुः अवदत् — शिष्यः पठेत्, न तु शयीत। तस्य पठनम् एव धर्मः। एकदा सः शिष्यः न अपठत्, वनम् अगच्छत् च। तत् श्रुत्वा गुरुः अक्रुध्यत्। रामेण तत् वचनम् श्रुतम्। सः चिन्तयत् — अहम् सदा पठेयम् इति।
sequence.translation: The teacher said — "A student should study, and not sleep. His studying alone is his dharma." One day that student did not study, and went to the forest. Hearing that, the teacher grew angry. Rāma heard those words. He thought — "I will always study."
sequence.teaches:
पठेत् and पठेयम् in one exchange, against अपठत् and अगच्छत्. पठनम् names
the act rather than the actor; श्रुत्वा and श्रुतम् are built from one root.

sequence.vyakhya: पठेत् पठेयम् अपठत् — एकः धातुः, त्रीणि रूपाणि।
sequence.vyakhya_en:
पठ् appears three times and means three different things by its ending
alone: पठेत् is what a student ought to do, पठेयम् is what this one resolves
to do, अपठत् is what he did not do. The root never changes.

sequence.sentence: कालियो नाम महासर्पः कालिन्दीनद्यां वसति स्म। तस्य विषेण जलं दूषितम् आसीत्। गावः पिबन्त्यः तत् जलम् पीत्वा मूर्च्छिताः अभवन्। तदा कृष्णः तरुम् आरुह्य नद्यां अपतत्। सः सर्पस्य फणेषु नृत्यन् तम् अदमयत्। एवम् कालियः कृष्णेन पराजितः।
sequence.translation: A great serpent named Kāliya lived in the Yamunā river. By his poison the water was polluted. The cows, while drinking, drank that water and fainted. Then Kṛṣṇa climbed a tree and fell into the river. He danced on the serpent's hoods and subdued it. Thus Kāliya was defeated by Kṛṣṇa.
sequence.teaches: लिट्-style past (वसति स्म as past habitual); passive क्त with आसीत् (past passive predicate); gerund आरुह्य + अपतत्; present participle (शतृ) पिबन्त्यः, नृत्यन् (action simultaneous with main verb); passive अदमयत् → पराजितः

notes.en: the thematic अ between root and ending
particle — with लट् makes past habitual ("used to dwell")

sequence.vyakhya: द्वे नवीने — शतृप्रत्ययः (लटः शतृशानचौ) पिबन्त्यः नृत्यन् च; स्म-सहितः लट् भूतार्थे। कर्मणिप्रयोगः त्रिवारम् — दूषितम् आसीत्, मूर्च्छिताः अभवन्, पराजितः। जलचरे युद्धम् वर्णयितुम् क्त्वा-ल्यपौ बहुशः।
sequence.vyakhya_en: Two new tools. First, **शतृ** (the active present participle — लटः शतृशानचौ, 3.2.124): पिबन्त्यः "while drinking" (fem. pl., simultaneous with अभवन्) and नृत्यन् "while dancing" (masc. sg., simultaneous with अदमयत्). The participle says the background action runs alongside the main verb — not before it (that's क्त्वा) and not after it. Second, **वसति स्म** — a present-tense verb with the particle स्म shifts into past habitual: "used to dwell." Passive क्त appears three times (दूषितम्, मूर्च्छिताः, पराजितः), anchoring the pattern from ex098. The gerunds आरुह्य → अपतत् chain the action sequence into one breath.

sequence.vyakhya_en: The genitive pair यस्य कस्य ("of whomsoever") waives the question of birth; अपि ("even/though") concedes it; and the verse turns on पूज्यते — "is honored," a passive, the same कर्मणि form you met in नरैः फलानि भुज्यन्ते. The sense: a man of merit (गुणवान्) is honored whatever his lineage. A relative clause and a passive, working together in real Sanskrit.

sequence.translation: In a certain village there lived a sage. The people asked him — "What should we do?" The sage said — "Practise giving, speak the truth. From giving comes happiness, and from untruth, sorrow. He who speaks truth is the best." These words were remembered by Rāma.

sequence.vyakhya_en: By अचो यत् (3.1.97) a root ending in a vowel takes the कृत्य affix यत्; so दा becomes देयम्, "to be given." Like every gerundive it governs case exactly as the passive does: the patient (धनम्) stands in the nominative, and an agent, if expressed, would stand in the instrumental. Here the recipient ब्राह्मणाय is in the dative (सम्प्रदान).

The genitive marks what one is sated *of*; the verb तृप्यति is shared across both halves. You now meet your own grammar — इ-stem, षष्ठी, कर्मधारय — in a real Pañcatantra verse.

sequence.translation: There is, on the bank of the Bhāgīrathī, a city named Pāṭaliputra. There lived a king called Sudarśana, endowed with every quality of a sovereign. One day that lord of the earth heard two verses being recited by someone.

sequence.vyakhya: कथामुखम् — अस्ति इति आरम्भः। समासबहुला गद्यरीतिः।
sequence.vyakhya_en:
Up to here the attested readings have been single-line maxims. This is
narrative, and it moves differently: three of its nouns are compounds
several members deep — भागीरथीतीरे, सर्वस्वामिगुणोपेतः, पाटलिपुत्रनामधेयं —
and unpacking them is most of the work of reading classical prose.

Take सर्वस्वामिगुणोपेतः from the back: उपेत, "endowed with"; endowed with
गुण, qualities; whose qualities — those of a सर्वस्वामिन्, an absolute
lord. English needs a clause where Sanskrit uses one word.

sequence.sentence: एकदा व्रजवासिनः इन्द्राय पूजाम् अकुर्वन्। कृष्णः अवदत् — "गोवर्धनाय पूजाम् कुरुत, न तु इन्द्राय।" जनाः तस्य वचनं श्रुत्वा तथा अकुर्वन्। तदा क्रुद्धः इन्द्रः मेघैः वर्षम् अप्रेरयत्। वर्षेण भयभीताः गावः च गोपाः च कृष्णम् अशरणम् अगच्छन्। कृष्णः तु गोवर्धनम् एव एकेन हस्तेन उद्धृत्य सप्त दिवसान् अधारयत्। एवम् गोवर्धनः कृष्णेन छत्रम् इव धृतः।
sequence.translation: Once the inhabitants of Vraja were performing a puja for Indra. Kṛṣṇa said — "Offer puja to Govardhana, not to Indra." The people, having heard his words, did so. Then angry Indra sent rain-clouds. Frightened by the rain, the cows and cowherds went to Kṛṣṇa as their refuge. But Kṛṣṇa alone, lifting Govardhana with one hand, held it for seven days. Thus Govardhana was held by Kṛṣṇa like an umbrella.
sequence.teaches: anīyar gerundive (implicitly: "the mountain is to-be-held"); upasarga + gerund उद्धृत्य; instrumental of cause (वर्षेण); accusative of duration (सप्त दिवसान्); simile (उपमा with इव); passive close (धृतः)

sequence.vyakhya: सर्वाधिकदीर्घा कथा — एका वाक्यपरम्परा। नवीनम् — उपमा (इव); अत्यन्तसंयोगे द्वितीया (सप्त दिवसान्); एकेन हस्तेन इति करणम्; क्रुद्धः इन्द्रः इति निष्ठाविशेषणम्। लोट् कुरुत इति विधौ; लङ् बहुशः कथावर्णने।
sequence.vyakhya_en: The longest katha reading, and it earns its length: five separate clauses, each moving the story. New arrivals: **इव** (the simile particle — Govardhana held "like an umbrella," छत्रम् इव); **accusative of duration** — सप्त दिवसान् "for seven days" (अत्यन्तसंयोगे द्वितीया, 2.3.5); the **instrumental of instrument with body-part** — एकेन हस्तेन "with one hand" (2.3.18); and the **dual coordinator** गावः च गोपाः च "both cows and cowherds." The closing passive (धृतः, 3.2.102) rounds the arc: episodes ex098–ex101 all end with a कर्मणि क्त — "was killed," "she saw," "was defeated," "was held" — each one a summary judgment on what just happened.

sequence.sentence: अ॒ग्निमी॑ळे पु॒रोहि॑तं य॒ज्ञस्य॑ दे॒वमृ॒त्विजं॑। होता॑रं रत्न॒धात॑मं॥

sequence.teaches: the accent marks appear for the first time — ॒ anudātta and ॑ for the udātta context. The grammar is already familiar: accusatives in apposition, a present verb

sequence.vyakhya: सर्वाणि कर्माणि अग्निविशेषणानि — द्वितीयायाम्। स्वराः उपरि अधश्च चिह्निताः।
sequence.vyakhya_en: Your first Vedic verse, and the grammar is already yours: ईळे "I praise" governs a string of accusatives all in apposition to अग्निम् — पुरोहितम्, देवम्, ऋत्विजम्, होतारम्, रत्नधातमम् — "I praise Agni: priest, god, minister, invoker, treasure-giver." The ONE new thing is accent: the underline ॒ marks anudātta (low pitch), the stroke ॑ marks the raised/svarita pitch. Each word's accent is shown in its padapāṭha (isolated) form — पुरोहितं appears word-alone as पुरः-हितम्. Read it aloud with the pitches: this is how the Veda is chanted.

the verse the king overhears. परोक्षार्थस्य दर्शकम् — an agent-noun takes

sequence.vyakhya: शास्त्रं लोचनम्। यस्य तत् नास्ति सः अन्धः।
sequence.vyakhya_en:
The verse says learning is an eye, and then does not soften it: whoever
lacks it is blind — अन्ध एव सः, with एव refusing the metaphor any room.

परोक्षार्थस्य दर्शकम् is worth slowing on. दर्शक is "one who shows", and
what it shows stands in the genitive rather than the accusative. That is
regular before a कृत् form and catches most readers the first time: the
sense is transitive, the case is not.

sequence.teaches: the second verse of the same hymn — अग्नि now stands as कर्तृ, and the agents come in the instrumental plural

sequence.vyakhya: अग्निः पूर्वैः नूतनैश्च ऋषिभिः ईड्यः; स देवान् इह आ वक्षति।
sequence.vyakhya_en: The same hymn's second verse, and the frame holds: अग्निः is now the कर्तृ (nominative — last verse he was अग्निम्, the object). The seers who praise him stand in the तृतीया (पूर्वेभिः, ऋषिभिः, नूतनैः — "by the ancient, by the seers, by the new"), the same instrumental "by" you met in नरैः. ईड्यः is a gerundive — "to-be-praised." Then सः (he) देवान् (the gods, acc.) आ … वक्षति — "may bring here." One word, अग्नि, you now know in two cases and with its accent.

sequence.sentence: अस्ति दाक्षिणात्ये जनपदे महिलारोप्यं नाम नगरम्। तत्र अमरशक्तिर् नाम राजा बभूव। तस्य त्रयः पुत्राः परमदुर्मेधसः आसन्। ततः राजा मन्त्रिणः आहूय उवाच — किम् अत्र कर्तव्यम् इति।
sequence.translation: There is, in a southern country, a city named Mahilāropya. There ruled a king named Amaraśakti. He had three sons, exceedingly dull-witted. Then the king, having summoned his ministers, said — "What is to be done here?"
sequence.teaches:
the Pañcatantra frame, in the same अस्ति … नाम नगरम् formula. Closes on
किम् अत्र कर्तव्यम् — a whole question with no verb in it.

notes.en: the same opening formula as the Hitopadeśa passage

sequence.vyakhya: अस्ति नाम नगरम् — कथामुखस्य रूढा रीतिः। हितोपदेशे अपि सैव।
sequence.vyakhya_en:
The same three words open this as opened the Hitopadeśa passage: अस्ति,
then a place, then नाम and the name. It is a formula, and recognising it
is worth more than parsing it — a classical story announces itself this way
and the reader can stop working until the कथा actually starts.

किम् अत्र कर्तव्यम् has no verb in it. कर्तव्यम् is a gerundive, "to-be-done",
and that is the whole predicate: what, here, is to-be-done. Sanskrit builds
a complete question out of a participle and two indeclinables.

sequence.sentence: कंसः नाम क्रूरः राजा कृष्णस्य मातुलः आसीत्। सः अचिन्तयत् — "अयम् बालः मया हन्तव्यः, अन्यथा सः माम् हनिष्यति।" तस्मात् सः अक्रूरम् गोकुलम् प्रैषयत्। अक्रूरः रथेन गत्वा कृष्णम् अवदत् — "मथुराम् आगच्छ, यतः तव दर्शनम् सर्वे इच्छन्ति।"
sequence.translation: A cruel king named Kaṃsa was Kṛṣṇa's maternal uncle. He thought — "This boy must be killed by me, otherwise he will kill me." Therefore he sent Akrūra to Gokula. Akrūra, having gone by chariot, said to Kṛṣṇa — "Come to Mathurā, for everyone desires the sight of you."
sequence.teaches: gerundive (अनीयर्/तव्य — हन्तव्यः "to-be-killed," with instrumental agent मया); future लृट् (हनिष्यति, इच्छन्ति present); causative प्रैषयत्; relative यतः-clause (reason); सम्बन्ध-षष्ठी (कृष्णस्य मातुलः, तव दर्शनम्)

sequence.vyakhya: महत् नवीनम् — कृत्यप्रत्ययः। हन्तव्यः इति तव्य (तव्यत्तव्यानीयरः), अर्थे "अवश्यं हननीयः"। कृत्ये कर्ता तृतीयायाम् (मया), कर्म प्रथमायाम् (बालः) — कर्मणिवत्। लृट् हनिष्यति इति भविष्यति; यतः इति हेतौ।
sequence.vyakhya_en: The big new arrival: the **gerundive** (कृत्य) — हन्तव्यः "(he) who must be killed," तव्य of √हन् (तव्यत्तव्यानीयरः, 3.1.96). It expresses necessity/obligation, and it governs case exactly like the passive: the agent goes to **instrumental** (मया "by me") and the patient to **nominative** (बालः). So "the boy is-to-be-killed by me" reads with मया … बालः … हन्तव्यः all in agreement. Against it stands the plain **future** हनिष्यति "he will kill" (लृट्, 3.3.13) — Kaṃsa weighs necessity against consequence. The reason-clause opens with यतः "because." This is the grammatical hinge from playful Gokula into the Mathurā confrontation.

sequence.vyakhya: अग्निना इति करणम्, रयिं पोषं च कर्म। दिवेदिवे इति आम्रेडितम्।
sequence.vyakhya_en: Now अग्नि steps into a third case: अग्निना, the तृतीया — "through Agni." You have met this stem as object (अग्निम्), as agent (अग्निः), and here as instrument (अग्निना): one इ-stem across three कारकas. Through Agni one wins रयिम् (wealth) and पोषम् (growth), both accusatives, qualified by यशसं वीरवत्तमं ("glorious, hero-rich"). दिवेदिवे — दिवे doubled — is an आम्रेडित, "day after day."

accusative — a numeral agreeing with वर्षाणि
duration — how long the studying lasts, not what it acts on

sequence.vyakhya: व्यतीते काले — सति सप्तमी। द्वादश वर्षाणि — कालद्वितीया।
sequence.vyakhya_en:
Two constructions here do work that English gives to conjunctions.
व्यतीते काले is a noun and a participle both in the locative, and together
they mean "when the time had passed" — no "when" anywhere in the Sanskrit.
Once recognised, it is everywhere in classical prose.

And द्वादश वर्षाणि is accusative, though nothing is being acted on. The
accusative also marks extent — how long, how far — so "for twelve years"
takes the same case as an object would.

source.curated: our simple Sanskrit; not from any single source

sequence.sentence: गुरुकुले द्वौ शिष्यौ आस्ताम्। एकः पटुः, अपरः पटुतरः। महाबुद्धिः बालः प्रश्नम् अपृच्छत्, तत् च सर्वैः अश्रूयत। गुरुः ततः तुष्टः अभवत्, श्रेष्ठाय च वरम् अददात्।
sequence.translation: In the teacher's school there were two students. One was clever, the other cleverer. The great-minded boy asked a question, and it was heard by all. The teacher thereupon was pleased, and gave a boon to the best one.
sequence.teaches:
a comparative (पटुतरः), a कर्मधारय (महाबुद्धिः), a passive (अश्रूयत), a
तसिल् adverb (ततः), a superlative (श्रेष्ठ) — five built words, one scene.

sequence.vyakhya: एकस्मिन्नाख्याने तरप्, कर्मधारयः, यक्, तसिल्, इष्ठन् — पञ्च शब्दप्रकाराः।
sequence.vyakhya_en:
Degrees and a passive, in one scene. पटुः is the plain grade; पटुतरः the
**comparative** — पटु + तर, "cleverer of the two"; श्रेष्ठ the **superlative**,
the इष्ठन्-grade of प्रशस्य, "best of all." महाबुद्धिः is a **compound** —
महती बुद्धिः यस्य, "he whose mind is great." अश्रूयत is a **passive**: the यक्
stem turns श्रु into "is heard," so तत् (the question) becomes the प्रथमा and
सर्वैः (all who hear) the तृतीया — the object rises to subject, the agent
steps back. And ततः is a **तसिल् adverb**, तद् + तस्, "from that → thereupon."

source.curated: complete verse, taken whole. Accent verbatim (traditional Devanagari svara) from sri-aurobindo.co.in

sequence.sentence: अग्ने॒ यं य॒ज्ञम॑ध्व॒रं वि॒श्वतः॑ परि॒भूरसि॑। स इद्दे॒वेषु॑ गच्छति॥
sequence.translation: O Agni, the sacrifice, the rite which you encompass on every side — that alone goes to the gods.
sequence.teaches: a Vedic relative-correlative यं … सः, the vocative अग्ने "O Agni," and असि "you are"

sequence.vyakhya: अग्ने इति सम्बोधनम्; यं यज्ञं परिभूः असि, स इत् देवेषु गच्छति।
sequence.vyakhya_en: A relative-correlative, Vedic style: यं … (यज्ञम् अध्वरं) … सः — "which sacrifice … that one." अग्ने is the सम्बोधन (vocative, "O Agni") — your fourth case-use of this one stem. असि is "you are," 2nd person (मध्यमपुरुष), matching the सम्बोधन. The sense: the rite that Agni encloses on every side (विश्वतः परिभूः) — *that one alone* (स इत्) reaches the gods (देवेषु, locative).

sequence.sentence: अथ विष्णुशर्मा नाम ब्राह्मणः अवदत् — देव, एतान् राजपुत्रान् षण्मासाभ्यन्तरे नीतिशास्त्रज्ञान् करिष्यामि। यदि न करोमि तदा देवः मम नाम त्यजतु।
sequence.translation: Then a brahmin named Viṣṇuśarman said — "Your Majesty, within six months I will make these princes knowers of the science of policy. If I do not, then let Your Majesty discard my name."
sequence.teaches:
the promise the Pañcatantra hangs on. नीतिशास्त्रज्ञान् is the second
accusative of "make X into Y"; त्यजतु stakes an oath.

notes.en: nominative — an अन्-stem, so the न् drops in the bare form

notes.en: object of त्यजतु — a different नाम from the indeclinable above
imperative, third person — a formal undertaking, not a command

notes.role: लोट् च — the imperative → त्यजतु

sequence.vyakhya: नाम इति द्विः — अव्ययं नाम, नाम्नः नाम च। संदर्भः भेदं दर्शयति।
sequence.vyakhya_en:
नाम appears twice and is not the same word. विष्णुशर्मा नाम ब्राह्मणः is
the indeclinable, "by name"; मम नाम त्यजतु is the noun नामन् in the
accusative, the thing to be discarded. Nothing but position and sense
separates them.

And note त्यजतु. A third-person imperative aimed at the king is not an
order — it is how a formal oath is staked: let my name be thrown away if I
fail. The grammar is imperative; the force is a wager.

sequence.sentence: कृष्णे गच्छति सति गोप्यः अतीव अरुदन्। याः गोप्यः कृष्णम् प्रेम्णा अपश्यन्, ताः सर्वाः शोकेन मग्नाः अभवन्। रथे स्थितः कृष्णः ताः रुदतीः दृष्ट्वा अपि न न्यवर्तत। तस्य हृदये तु ताः एव सर्वदा अवसन्।
sequence.translation: When Kṛṣṇa was leaving, the gopīs wept bitterly. Those gopīs who used to look upon Kṛṣṇa with love — all of them were sunk in grief. Kṛṣṇa, seated in the chariot, though he saw them weeping, did not turn back. Yet in his heart they alone dwelt always.
sequence.teaches: locative absolute (सति-सप्तमी — कृष्णे गच्छति सति, 2.3.37); relative-correlative याः…ताः over a full clause; present participle as object (रुदतीः "weeping ones"); gerund दृष्ट्वा with concessive अपि

sequence.vyakhya: अधिकरणं त्रिविधम् इह — सति-सप्तमी (कृष्णे गच्छति सति) कालार्थे; रथे हृदये इति देशाधिकरणे। याः…ताः इति वाक्यद्वये सम्बन्धः। रुदतीः इति शतृ कर्मणि (ताः रुदतीः)। दृष्ट्वा अपि इति अनुमत्यर्थे — "दृष्ट्वापि न न्यवर्तत"।
sequence.vyakhya_en: Three locatives, three jobs. The **locative absolute** (सति-सप्तमी, 2.3.37) sets the scene in time — कृष्णे गच्छति सति "Kṛṣṇa being-in-the-act-of-going," i.e. "as Kṛṣṇa was leaving": a whole subordinate clause folded into two locative words. Ordinary locatives of place follow — रथे "in the chariot," हृदये "in the heart" (2.3.36). The relative-correlative याः … ताः now spans a full clause ("those gopīs who used to look on him — they all sank in grief"). And the शतृ participle appears for the first time **as an accusative object** — ताः रुदतीः "them, the weeping ones." दृष्ट्वा अपि "even having seen" gives the concessive: he saw, yet did not turn.

sequence.sentence: अ॒ग्निर्होता॑ क॒विक्र॑तुः स॒त्यश्चि॒त्रश्र॑वस्तमः। दे॒वो दे॒वेभि॒रा ग॑मत्॥
sequence.translation: Agni the invoker, wise in will, true, most brilliant in fame — a god, may he come with the gods.
sequence.teaches: nominative epithets predicated without a verb, a बहुव्रीहि compound, and the instrumental of accompaniment

sequence.vyakhya: होता कविक्रतुः सत्यः चित्रश्रवस्तमः देवः — सर्वाणि अग्निविशेषणानि प्रथमायाम्। देवेभिः इति सहार्थे तृतीया।
sequence.vyakhya_en: Verse 1 strung accusatives; this one strings NOMINATIVES. होता, कविक्रतुः, सत्यः, चित्रश्रवस्तमः, देवः — all प्रथमा, all naming अग्निः (predication, no copula needed). कविक्रतुः is a बहुव्रीहि: "(one) whose क्रतु is a sage's." Then देवेभिः is the तृतीया of accompaniment — "with the gods" — the सह-sense you met in पुत्रेण सह. आ गमत्: "may he come hither."

sequence.translation: Whatever good you will do for the worshipper, O Agni — that, indeed, is your truth, O Aṅgiras.
sequence.teaches: दाशुषे "for the giver" as सम्प्रदान in the चतुर्थी, and करिष्यसि in the future

sequence.vyakhya: यत् भद्रं दाशुषे करिष्यसि, तत् तव सत्यम्। दाशुषे इति सम्प्रदाने चतुर्थी।
sequence.vyakhya_en: A यत्…तत् sentence with two new turns. दाशुषे is the सम्प्रदान — the dative (चतुर्थी), "for the worshipper," the same "for whom" case you met in नमो देवेभ्यः. करिष्यसि is a FUTURE (लृट्), "you will do" — √कृ now in the future, 2nd person. Two vocatives frame it: अग्ने and अङ्गिरः (a name of Agni). The sense: whatever blessing you will do for the giver — *that* is your truth.

sequence.sentence: यः कंसः चिरम् कृष्णस्य वधम् इच्छति स्म, सः एव अधुना भयेन कम्पते। कृष्णः मथुराम् प्रविश्य रङ्गभूमौ मल्लान् अहन्। ततः सः उच्चासनात् कंसम् आकृष्य भूमौ अपातयत्। यम् राजानम् सर्वे जनाः अबिभयुः, सः कृष्णेन क्षणेन एव हतः। एवम् अधर्मस्य अन्तः, धर्मस्य च जयः अभवत्।
sequence.translation: He who for long had wished for Kṛṣṇa's death — that very one now trembles with fear. Kṛṣṇa, having entered Mathurā, killed the wrestlers in the arena. Then he dragged Kaṃsa down from his high throne and threw him to the ground. The king whom all people had feared — he was killed by Kṛṣṇa in but a moment. Thus came the end of unrighteousness, and the victory of dharma.
sequence.teaches: climax — two relative-correlatives (यः…सः on the subject, यम्…सः on the object); अपादान (भयस्य source → उच्चासनात् ablative, अबिभयुः with 5th); causative अपातयत्; षष्ठी of object with कृत् (कृष्णस्य वधम्, 2.3.65); passive close (हतः)

sequence.vyakhya: कथायाः शिखरम् — द्वौ सम्बन्धौ यद्-तद्। कर्तरि यः…सः (यः इच्छति स्म सः कम्पते); कर्मणि यम्…सः (यं अबिभयुः सः हतः)। अपादानम् द्विधा — उच्चासनात् (departure), भयस्य हेतुः भी-धातुना अबिभयुः। वधम् इति कृत्, तत्र कर्म षष्ठ्याम् (कृष्णस्य वधम्)। अन्ते कर्मणि हतः — कथार्धम् सर्वम् कर्मणि समाप्यते।
sequence.vyakhya_en: The climax, and it gathers everything. Two relative-correlatives frame it, one on each axis: यः … सः on the **subject** ("he who long wished Kṛṣṇa's death — that one now trembles") and यम् … सः on the **object** ("the king whom all feared — he was killed"). Two ablatives of separation: उच्चासनात् "from the high throne" (2.3.28) and the fear-source folded into अबिभयुः. The action-noun वधम् "killing" takes its object in the **genitive** — कृष्णस्य वधम् "the killing OF Kṛṣṇa" (2.3.65, the कृत्-षष्ठी). The arc that began with butter and a rope ends as it must, in the passive: हतः "was killed" — and the whole Kṛṣṇa-childhood sequence closes on its grammatical signature, the कर्मणि क्त, now carrying the weight of a death rather than a game.

sequence.vyakhya: वयं धिया नमो भरन्तः दिवेदिवे त्वा उप आ इमसि। एमसि इति उत्तमपुरुषबहुवचनम्।
sequence.vyakhya_en: The worshippers speak now in their own voice: वयम् "we," and एमसि (उप…आ…इमसि) "we come" — a 1st-person PLURAL verb (उत्तमपुरुष बहुवचन), the same person you met as -मि in गच्छामि, now plural. To you (त्वा, accusative) we come, day by day (दिवेदिवे), at night and dawn (दोषावस्तः), in thought (धिया, तृतीया of means), bearing homage (नमः भरन्तः). A whole sentence of grammar you already hold.

sequence.sentence: गुरुणा शिष्याः पाठ्यन्ते। तैः शास्त्राणि पठ्यन्ते, वचनानि च श्रूयन्ते। गुरुः तान् द्रष्टुम् इच्छति। श्वः ते ग्रामम् गमिष्यन्ति। तत्र धनम् धान्यम् च लप्स्यन्ते। नद्याः तीरे तिष्ठन्ति, जलम् पिबन्ति च।
sequence.translation: The students are taught by the teacher. By them the treatises are read, and the sayings are heard. The teacher wishes to see them. Tomorrow they will go to the village. There they will obtain wealth and grain. They stand on the river's bank, and drink water.
sequence.teaches:
four passives against two actives. The same students appear as शिष्याः,
तैः, ते and तान् — the case follows what the verb's ending points at.

sequence.vyakhya: तैः पठ्यन्ते, ते गच्छन्ति। एकः कर्ता, द्वे विभक्ती।
sequence.vyakhya_en:
The same students appear four times and are named three different ways.
शिष्याः when the passive points at them, तैः when the passive points past
them at what they read, ते when the verb is active and points at them
again, तान् when someone else's verb points at them.

Nothing about the students changed. Each time, the case answers one
question: has the verb's ending already said this? If yes, प्रथमा. If no,
whatever case the role calls for.

sequence.teaches: accusative epithets continuing from the previous verse, with अध्वराणां "of the rites" in the genitive plural and स्वे दमे "in his own home" in the locative

genitive plural — that over which one rules

षष्ठी शेषे → ऋतस्य

sequence.vyakhya: राजन्तं गोपां दीदिविं वर्धमानं — सर्वाणि कर्माणि (पूर्वस्या ऋचः त्वा-शब्दस्य विशेषणानि)। अध्वराणाम् ऋतस्य च षष्ठी; स्वे दमे इति सप्तमी।
sequence.vyakhya_en: This verse has no new finite verb — it continues verse 7's "to you we come," piling accusative epithets onto that त्वा: राजन्तम् (ruling), गोपाम् (guardian), दीदिविम् (shining), वर्धमानम् (growing). Two participles (राजन्तम् active, वर्धमानम् middle) decline like nouns in the accusative. The genitives अध्वराणाम् (over the rites) and ऋतस्य (of truth) mark domain; स्वे दमे — सप्तमी — locates it: "in his own home." Cases you hold, stacked into Vedic praise.

sequence.sentence: महाबलः नृपः सभाम् आगच्छत्। तस्य पार्श्वे मन्त्रिपुरोहितौ आस्ताम्। नीलाम्बरः दूतः प्रविश्य उपसभम् अतिष्ठत्। सः महाबलम् अवदत् — शत्रुसेना पराजिता, राष्ट्रम् च रक्षितम्।
sequence.translation: The mighty king came to the assembly. At his side were the minister-and-priest. A blue-clad messenger, having entered, stood near the assembly. He said to the mighty one — "The enemy-army is defeated, and the kingdom protected."
sequence.teaches:
the four compound types again, none of them new: महाबलः (बहुव्रीहि),
मन्त्रिपुरोहितौ (द्वन्द्व), उपसभम् (अव्ययीभाव), शत्रुसेना (तत्पुरुष).

notes.en: possessive — neither member is the head; it names the one who HAS great strength

अनेकमन्यपदार्थे — several words denoting ANOTHER thing (the possessor) form a बहुव्रीहि

passive — agrees with शत्रुसेना, no finite verb
the thing protected — subject of the passive predicate
the क्त निष्ठा suffix — passive, "was protected"

sequence.vyakhya: चत्वारः समासाः एकस्मिन् दृश्ये — महाबलः, मन्त्रिपुरोहितौ, उपसभम्, शत्रुसेना।
sequence.vyakhya_en:
All four kinds in one scene, and each doing ordinary work. महाबलः is a
बहुव्रीहि — not "great" and not "strength" but the one who HAS great strength,
the king. मन्त्रिपुरोहितौ is a द्वन्द्व, minister and priest taken as a pair.
उपसभम् is an अव्ययीभाव, उप carrying it and the whole going indeclinable. And
शत्रुसेना is a तत्पुरुष — शत्रोः सेना, the enemy's army — whose defeat the
passive participle पराजिता reports without a finite verb.

sequence.sentence: कस्मिंश्चित् वने भासुरको नाम सिंहः वसति स्म। सः बलवान् आसीत्, किन्तु अतीव क्रूरः। प्रतिदिनम् सः बहून् पशून् अहन्। तेन सर्वे मृगाः भयेन कम्पन्ते स्म। ते मिलित्वा सिंहम् ऊचुः — "हे स्वामिन्, मा सर्वान् पशून् हन्। वयम् एव प्रतिदिनम् एकम् पशुम् तव आहाराय प्रेषयिष्यामः।"
sequence.translation: In a certain forest there lived a lion named Bhāsuraka. He was strong, but exceedingly cruel. Every day he killed many animals. Because of this all the beasts trembled with fear. They, having gathered, said to the lion — "O master, do not kill all the animals. We ourselves will send one animal every day for your food."
sequence.teaches: the fable opens: कस्मिंश्चित् as an indefinite locative, the prohibitive मा with लङ् in मा हन्, a first-person plural future प्रेषयिष्यामः, आहाराय as a dative of purpose, and ऊचुः in the perfect

sequence.vyakhya: नूतनकथारम्भः — पञ्चतन्त्रात्। कस्मिंश्चित् वने इति लोकप्रसिद्धम् आख्यानारम्भपदम्। मा हन् इति प्रतिषेधे लुङ् अनद्यतनः अनागमकः। आहाराय इति तादर्थ्ये चतुर्थी; प्रेषयिष्यामः इति लृट् उत्तमपुरुषबहुवचने।
sequence.vyakhya_en: A new story begins — from the Pañcatantra, and it opens with the formula every Sanskrit tale is built on: कस्मिंश्चित् वने "in a certain forest" (कः + चित् = the indefinite "some"). One genuinely new construction: the **prohibitive** — मा with an augmentless past (मा … हन् "do not kill"), the standard way Sanskrit says "don't." Against it stands the animals' **future promise** — प्रेषयिष्यामः "we will send" (लृट्, 1st plural). The dative आहाराय "for food" is the dative of purpose (तादर्थ्य). All the rest — past tenses, gerund मिलित्वा, instrumental of cause भयेन — is grammar you already own, now carrying a fable instead of a god.

sequence.sentence: स नः॑ पि॒तेव॑ सू॒नवेऽग्ने॑ सूपाय॒नो भ॑व। सच॑स्वा नः स्व॒स्तये॑॥
sequence.translation: Be to us, O Agni, easy of approach, as a father to his son; abide with us for our well-being.
sequence.teaches: the simile पिता इव "like a father," datives of the one addressed — सूनवे, नः, स्वस्तये — and the imperatives भव and सचस्व

notes.role: चतुर्थी सम्प्रदाने → नः ("for us")

notes.text: padapāṭha splits पिता-इव; पिता (nom, the ऋ-stem you met) + इव "like"

notes.en: recipient — "(as a father) to a son"

notes.role: चतुर्थी सम्प्रदाने → सूनवे (an उ-stem dative, गुण → सूनवे, like अग्नये)
सम्बोधने च → अग्ने

notes.text: padapāṭha splits सु-उपायन; सु "well, easy" + उपायन "approach"

notes.en: predicate adjective of भव — "be (one) easy to approach"
imperative — "be!" (the command mood you met in गच्छतु)

notes.role: लोट् च — imperative → भव (2sg "be!")
लोट् च — imperative → सचस्व

notes.text: नः again — here "with us" (object/goal of सचस्व)

notes.role: चतुर्थी सम्प्रदाने → स्वस्तये (an इ-stem dative, like अग्नये)

sequence.vyakhya: पिता सूनवे इव, अग्ने नः सूपायनः भव; नः स्वस्तये सचस्व। चतुर्थ्यः बह्व्यः — सूनवे नः स्वस्तये।
sequence.vyakhya_en: The hymn closes with a prayer, dense with the चतुर्थी (dative): नः "for us," सूनवे "to a son," स्वस्तये "for well-being" — three datives, all the "for whom" case (सम्प्रदान). The heart is a simile: पिता इव सूनवे — "as a father (is) to a son." Two imperatives (लोट्) carry the request: भव "be!" and सचस्व "abide!" — the command mood you met in गच्छतु, here in real Vedic. With this you have read the whole first hymn of the Ṛgveda, end to end, with its accent.

sequence.vyakhya_en: A new hymn, a new god — but the grammar is the invocation pattern you just met closing hymn 1. वायो is the सम्बोधन (vocative of the उ-stem वायु, गुण → वायो like गुरो), and it is answered by a volley of imperatives (लोट्): आ याहि "come!", पाहि "drink!", श्रुधि "hear!". The Somas (सोमाः, nominative plural) stand ready (अरंकृताः); drink *of them* — तेषाम्, a genitive (षष्ठी) in the partitive sense — and hear the call (हवम्, accusative). The whole verse is address + command, the heartbeat of Vedic prayer.

sequence.sentence: एकदा शशकस्य वारः आगच्छत्। सः बुद्धिमान् शशकः चिरम् विचिन्त्य एकम् उपायम् अकरोत्। सः मन्दम् मन्दम् सिंहस्य समीपम् अगच्छत्। क्रुद्धः सिंहः अपृच्छत् — "किमर्थम् त्वम् विलम्बेन आगतः?" शशकः अवदत् — "मार्गे अन्यः बलवान् सिंहः माम् अरुणत्। सः त्वाम् एव स्वामिनम् न मन्यते।" तत् श्रुत्वा क्रुद्धः सिंहः तम् द्रष्टुम् इच्छति स्म।
sequence.translation: One day the rabbit's turn came. That clever rabbit, after thinking for a long time, devised a plan. He went very slowly toward the lion. The angry lion asked — "Why have you come late?" The rabbit said — "On the road another strong lion stopped me. He does not regard you alone as master." Having heard that, the angry lion wished to see him.

sequence.vyakhya: संवादः दीर्घतरः। किमर्थम् इति हेतुप्रश्ने; आगतः इति निष्ठा कर्तरि ("त्वम् आगतः")। माम् अरुणत् इति रुध्-धातोः सप्तमगणे लङ्। स्वामिनम् इति द्विकर्मके मन्यतेः अभिन्ननिर्देशे। द्रष्टुम् इच्छति इति तुमुन् इष्-धातुना।
sequence.vyakhya_en: The dialogue lengthens — the trick is told, not just narrated. New touches: किमर्थम् "why? for what purpose?" (the interrogative of cause); the past participle as a finite-like **predicate** — त्वम् … आगतः "you have come" (क्त standing in for "you came/are come"); and a double-accusative with मन्यते — त्वाम् स्वामिनम् न मन्यते "does not regard you AS master," the object and its predicate-complement both accusative. The infinitive द्रष्टुम् इच्छति "wishes to see" closes on the hook that will spring the trap. Everything else is consolidation: four लङ् pasts, two gerunds (विचिन्त्य, श्रुत्वा), locatives, the मतुप् adjectives बलवान्/बुद्धिमान्.

sequence.vyakhya_en: Hymn 1 ended with "we come"; here the worshippers are NAMED — जरितारः, "the singers," the agents (कर्तृ, an ऋ-stem nominative plural like कर्तारः). They praise (जरन्ते, 3rd-person plural) you (त्वाम्, accusative) with hymns (उक्थेभिः) — the तृतीया of means, the same "with/by" you met in नरैः and धिया. Two epithets describe them: सुतसोमाः ("Soma-pressed," a बहुव्रीहि) and अहर्विदः ("day-knowers"). All grammar you hold.

sequence.vyakhya_en: A feminine subject leads: धेना ("stream," an आ-stem feminine like विद्या), with two feminine adjectives agreeing — प्रपृञ्चती ("nourishing") and उरूची ("broad"). It is तव ("yours," genitive) and it जिगाति ("goes") दाशुषे ("to the worshipper," dative). The last word shows a second flavour of the dative: सोमपीतये — *for the purpose of* Soma-drinking. One case (चतुर्थी), two senses: "to whom" (दाशुषे) and "for what" (सोमपीतये).

sequence.sentence: शशकः सिंहम् एकम् कूपम् अनयत्। "अत्र सः शत्रुः वसति" इति सः अवदत्। सिंहः कूपम् अपश्यत्। जले तस्य एव प्रतिबिम्बम् आसीत्, किन्तु सः तत् अन्यम् सिंहम् अमन्यत। क्रुद्धः सः गर्जितुम् आरभत। कूपात् प्रतिशब्दः श्रूयते स्म। तेन सः अतीव अक्रुध्यत्। "अहम् एनम् हनिष्यामि" इति उक्त्वा सः कूपे अपतत्। तत्र मग्नः सिंहः अम्रियत। एवम् बुद्ध्या शशकः सर्वान् मृगान् अरक्षत्। बलम् बुद्धिः च — तयोः बुद्धिः एव श्रेष्ठा।
sequence.translation: The rabbit led the lion to a well. "Your enemy lives here," he said. The lion looked into the well. In the water was his own reflection, but he took it for another lion. Enraged, he began to roar. An echo was heard from the well. At that he grew still angrier. Saying "I will kill him," he leapt into the well. Sunk there, the lion died. Thus by his wit the rabbit saved all the beasts. Strength and intelligence — of the two, intelligence is the better.
sequence.teaches:
the close of the सिंह-शशक story. Eight past verbs against one future —
हनिष्यामि, the thing the lion intends and does not accomplish.

sequence.vyakhya: बलवान् सिंहः मृतः, बुद्धिमान् शशकः जीवति। न बलेन, बुद्ध्या जयः।
sequence.vyakhya_en:
The lion never sees another lion. He sees himself and cannot tell, and the
echo he answers is his own voice returning. The story spends its whole
length on that one joke, and the last line names it: बलम् बुद्धिः च, and
of the two, बुद्धिः.

Nine finite verbs here and eight of them are past — अनयत्, अपश्यत्,
अमन्यत, अक्रुध्यत्, अपतत्, अम्रियत, अरक्षत्, आसीत्. Against them stand
वसति and श्रूयते inside quoted or reported speech, where the present holds,
and हनिष्यामि, the only future in the passage: the one thing the lion
intends and does not accomplish.

sequence.vyakhya: इन्द्रवायू इति द्वन्द्वः द्विवचने; आ गतम् इति द्विवचनलोट्; वाम् इति द्विवचनम्। द्वौ देवौ, द्विवचनम्।
sequence.vyakhya_en: The DUAL arrives — Sanskrit's third number, for exactly two. The pair इन्द्रवायू is a द्वन्द्व compound ("Indra and Vāyu") in the dual (द्विवचन, 1.4.22), and everything addressed to them is dual too: आ गतम् "come, *you two*" (a dual imperative), and वाम् "you two" (the dual of युष्मद्). Between, सुताः ("the pressed Somas") and इन्दवः ("the drops") are plural subjects. Singular, plural, and now dual — the वचन triad is complete, here in real Vedic.

sequence.vyakhya: वायुः इन्द्रश्च — द्वौ; चेतथः यातम् इति द्विवचने तिङन्ते। सर्वं द्विवचनम्।
sequence.vyakhya_en: The dual you just met now drives the VERB. वायो and इन्द्रः, joined by च, are two — so चेतथः ("you two perceive") is a dual finite verb, तौ ("you two") is the dual pronoun, यातम् ("come, you two") the dual imperative, and वाजिनीवसू a dual vocative epithet. Everything addressed to the pair is dual. They take note सुतानाम् — "of the pressed Somas," a partitive genitive (षष्ठी). The whole verse is a drill in द्विवचन.

sequence.sentence: कस्मिंश्चित् ग्रामे एकः ब्राह्मणः वसति स्म। तस्य गृहे एकः नकुलः आसीत्। ब्राह्मणस्य पत्नी बालम् रक्षन्ती गृहे तिष्ठति स्म। एकदा सा जलम् आनेतुम् बहिः अगच्छत्। तस्मिन् काले एकः कृष्णसर्पः बालस्य समीपम् आगच्छत्। तम् दृष्ट्वा नकुलः सर्पेण सह अयुध्यत। तेन सर्पः हतः, नकुलस्य मुखम् च रक्तेन लिप्तम् आसीत्। पत्नी प्रत्यागच्छत्। रक्तानि नकुलस्य मुखे दृष्ट्वा सा अचिन्तयत् — "अनेन मम बालः खादितः" इति। क्रुद्धा सा घटम् तस्य उपरि अक्षिपत्। नकुलः अम्रियत। गृहम् प्रविश्य सा बालम् सुप्तम् अपश्यत्, हतम् सर्पम् च। तदा सा अतीव अरोदीत् — "अहम् मूढा, विचार्य न कृतवती" इति।
sequence.translation: In a certain village there lived a brahmin. In his house was a mongoose. The brahmin's wife, guarding the child, used to stay at home. One day she went out to fetch water. At that time a black snake came near the child. Seeing it, the mongoose fought with the snake. By that the snake was killed, and the mongoose's mouth was smeared with blood. The wife returned. Seeing the blood on the mongoose's mouth, she thought — "My child has been eaten by this one." Enraged, she threw a pot upon him. The mongoose died. Entering the house, she saw the child asleep, and the snake killed. Then she wept bitterly — "I am a fool; I did not act after thinking."
sequence.teaches:
the mongoose story, told in participles. The tragedy turns on one of them:
रक्तानि दृष्ट्वा, seeing the blood, and what the wife concludes from it.

sequence.vyakhya: रक्तानि दृष्ट्वा सा अमन्यत। दर्शनम् सत्यम्, अनुमानम् मिथ्या।
sequence.vyakhya_en:
Everything the wife sees is true. There is blood on the mongoose's mouth.
What she adds is the inference, and the story hangs the whole tragedy on
the gap between them — रक्तानि दृष्ट्वा, seeing the blood, and then
खादितः, "he has been eaten", which she never saw at all.

The participles carry it. हतः, लिप्तम्, सुप्तम्, हतम् are all states
someone else could have verified; खादितः is the one she supplied. And the
last word answers it: कृतवती, the active past participle — not something
done to her, but the thing she did.

sequence.vyakhya_en: The pair is called again — यातम्, "come, you two" — but now with a goal: उप … निष्कृतम्, "up to the prepared offering," where the goal of motion takes the accusative (द्वितीया, just as a destination does). सुन्वतः ("of the presser") is a genitive: whose offering it is. धिया ("by thought") is the instrumental of means you already hold. And the address नरा is नरौ — the DUAL of नर, the very first noun you ever declined, now standing in the vocative dual.

sequence.vyakhya_en: A new divine pair enters — Mitra and Varuṇa. Here they are OBJECTS: मित्रम् … वरुणम् च, accusatives, "I call (हुवे, 1st-person singular) Mitra and Varuṇa," each with its epithet (पूतदक्षम् "pure-skilled," रिशादसम् "foe-destroying"). They jointly perfect धियं घृताचीम् ("the luminous thought," accusative) — and साधन्ता, "the two who perfect," is a participle in the DUAL, agreeing with the pair. The dual now appears even on a participle.

sequence.sentence: नद्याः तीरे वणिजः वसन्ति स्म। तेषाम् गृहेषु धनम् धान्यम् च आसीत्। एकदा एकः वणिक् दूरम् देशम् गन्तुम् ऐच्छत्। मित्राणि तम् अवदन् — मार्गः दीर्घः, मा गच्छ इति। किन्तु सः अशृणोत् न। श्वः गमिष्यामि इति उक्त्वा सः रात्रौ यानम् असज्जयत्। प्रभाते तेन मित्राणि त्यक्तानि, नगरम् च त्यक्तम्।
sequence.translation: On the bank of a river lived merchants. In their houses were wealth and grain. One day one merchant wished to go to a distant country. His friends said to him — "The road is long; do not go." But he did not listen. Saying "I will go tomorrow," he made ready a cart in the night. At dawn the friends were left behind by him, and the city too was left.
sequence.teaches:
a merchant leaves against advice. Closes on तेन मित्राणि त्यक्तानि — two
participles and an instrumental agent, with no finite verb.

sequence.vyakhya: मा गच्छ इति उक्तम्, तथापि सः अगच्छत्। तेन मित्राणि त्यक्तानि।
sequence.vyakhya_en:
The last sentence has no finite verb in it. त्यक्तानि and त्यक्तम् are
participles, and they carry the whole statement — the friends left, the
city left, and तेन telling you by whom.

Classical Sanskrit prefers this to a past-tense verb, which is why so much
narrative reads as a chain of participles with the agent in the
instrumental. Once मित्राणि त्यक्तानि stops needing to be translated as a
passive, it starts reading as ordinary past narration.

sequence.vyakhya: ऋतेन इति करणम्; मित्रावरुणौ ऋतावृधौ ऋतस्पृशा — द्विवचनसम्बोधनानि; बृहन्तं क्रतुम् आशाथे — लिटि द्विवचनम्।
sequence.vyakhya_en: Now Mitra-Varuṇa are ADDRESSED, as a single dual द्वन्द्व: मित्रावरुणौ (vocative dual), with two dual epithets, ऋतावृधौ ("Truth-increasers") and ऋतस्पृशा ("Truth-touchers"). The line opens with ऋतेन — "by the Truth," the instrumental of means. And the verb is new: आशाथे, "you two have attained" — a PERFECT (लिट्, the tense of चकार) in the DUAL. Tense, number, and compound all converge on the pair.

sequence.vyakhya_en: The hymn closes with the pair as SUBJECTS, all in the nominative dual: कवी ("two seers"), मित्रावरुणा (now agents, not addressed), तुविजाता ("mightily born"), उरुक्षया ("wide-dwelling"). They दधाते — "the two hold" — a present DUAL verb of √धा, the same root as ददाति "gives." For us (नः, dative) they hold दक्षम् अपसम् ("a working skill," accusative). You have now read the whole second hymn, and through it drilled the entire dual — noun, pronoun, adjective, participle, and verb across three tenses.

sequence.sentence: कस्मिंश्चित् देशे धनवान् राजा आसीत्। तस्य पिता वृद्धः दरिद्रः च अभवत्। राजा पितरम् न अपश्यत्, न च तम् अस्मरत्। एकदा भगवान् मुनिः सभाम् आगच्छत्। सः राजानम् अवदत् — पितरि भक्तिः एव धर्मः। यः पितरम् त्यजति सः राज्ञः नाम न अर्हति। तत् श्रुत्वा राज्ञा शिरः अवनतम्। ततः सः पितुः गृहम् अगच्छत्, तस्य पादौ च अस्पृशत्।
sequence.translation: In a certain country there was a wealthy king. His father had become old and poor. The king did not look at his father, nor did he remember him. One day the Blessed One, a sage, came to the assembly. He said to the king — "Devotion toward one's father is dharma itself. He who abandons his father does not deserve the name of king." Having heard that, the king's head was bowed. Then he went to his father's house, and touched his feet.
sequence.teaches:
a king who forgets his father. पितृ appears in four cases across the
story — पिता, पितरम्, पितरि, पितुः.

sequence.vyakhya: पिता पितरम् पितरि पितुः — चतुर्षु स्थानेषु एकः जनः।
sequence.vyakhya_en:
One man, four shapes: पिता when he is named, पितरम् when the king fails to
look at him, पितरि when devotion is owed toward him, पितुः when his house
is meant. Nothing about the father changes across the story.

The king does the same — राजा, राजानम्, राज्ञः, राज्ञा — and the last of
those, राज्ञा शिरः अवनतम्, has no finite verb: a participle and an
instrumental agent, which is how classical narrative most often reports
what someone did.

sequence.vyakhya_en: A new hymn, a new dual pair: the अश्विन्s, the twin horsemen, addressed throughout in the dual vocative — अश्विना, द्रवत्पाणी ("swift-handed"), शुभस्पती ("lords of bliss"), पुरुभुजा ("of many bounties"). They are asked to चनस्यतम् — "take pleasure, you two" — a DUAL imperative (लोट्), the same dual-of-command you met as आ गतम् in rd020. What they enjoy is यज्वरीः इषः, "the worshipper's offerings," an accusative PLURAL object (कर्मन्). The dual you drilled across RV 1.2 now carries to a fresh pair.

sequence.vyakhya: अश्विना नरा धिष्ण्या — सम्बोधनद्विवचनम्; शवीरया धिया — तृतीयैकवचनं करणे; गिरः — द्वितीयाबहुवचनं कर्मणि; वनतम् — लोटि मध्यमपुरुषद्विवचनम्।
sequence.vyakhya_en: The Aśvins again, addressed as नरा — which is नरौ, the dual of नर, the first noun this whole reader ever declined, now standing in a Vedic hymn. They are to वनतम् ("win, you two," dual imperative) the गिरः, "songs of praise" (accusative plural object). The means is शवीरया धिया, "with forceful thought" — an INSTRUMENTAL (करण, तृतीया), the same धी "thought" you met as धिया in rd014. One verse braids three threads you already hold: the dual address, the accusative object, and the instrument of means.

sequence.sentence: राजा वनम् गच्छन् एकम् मुनिम् अपश्यत्। मुनिः वृक्षस्य अधः उपविशन् शिष्यान् अवदत् — कर्तव्यम् धर्मम् जानीत। राज्ञः भ्राता अपि तत्र आसीत्। सः पितुः वचनम् स्मरन् मुनिम् अपृच्छत् — किम् मया करणीयम्। मुनिः अवदत् — भ्रातरम् रक्ष, राजानम् सेव, पितरम् च मा त्यज। एतत् त्रयम् सर्वदा स्मरणीयम्। तत् श्रुत्वा भ्रातरौ शान्तौ अभवताम्।
sequence.translation: The king, going to the forest, saw a sage. The sage, sitting beneath a tree, said to his students — "Know the dharma that is to be done." The king's brother was there too. He, remembering his father's words, asked the sage — "What is to be done by me?" The sage said — "Protect your brother, serve the king, and do not abandon your father. These three are always to be remembered." Having heard that, the two brothers became calm.
sequence.teaches:

and three gerundives stating obligation with no verb: कर्तव्यम्, करणीयम्,
स्मरणीयम्.

sequence.vyakhya: गच्छन् उपविशन् स्मरन् — त्रीणि शतृ-रूपाणि। कर्तव्यम् करणीयम् स्मरणीयम् — त्रीणि कृत्य-रूपाणि।
sequence.vyakhya_en:
Three participles here do what English does with "while": राजा वनम् गच्छन्
is "the king, as he went to the forest". None of them is the sentence's
main verb, and none needs a conjunction.

Then three gerundives state obligation without any verb at all —
कर्तव्यम्, करणीयम्, स्मरणीयम्. Two different affixes, तव्य and अनीयर्,
with no difference in sense; a writer picks whichever fits the line.
किम् मया करणीयम् is the whole question: what, by me, is to-be-done.

sequence.vyakhya_en: The triplet to the Aśvins closes with a NOMINATIVE string describing the offering: युवाकवः सुताः वृक्तबर्हिषः — "the pressed (soma), yearning for you, with sacred grass strewn." These are predicates: the rite is ready. The pair, addressed as दस्रा ("wondrous"), नासत्या ("truthful"), रुद्रवर्तनी ("of Rudra's path"), are bidden आ यातम् — "come, you two" — the very dual imperative you first met as आ गतम् in rd020. The Aśvin hymn is complete.

sequence.vyakhya: इन्द्र चित्रभानो — सम्बोधने एकवचनम्; आ याहि — लोटि मध्यमपुरुषैकवचनम् (द्विवचनयातमः प्रतियोगि); सुताः इमे त्वायवः पूतासः — प्रथमाबहुवचने कर्तृविशेषणानि; अण्वीभिः तना — तृतीया करणे।
sequence.vyakhya_en: The hymn turns from the pair to a single god, and the grammar turns with it: इन्द्र is a SINGULAR vocative, and he is bidden आ याहि — "come!" — a 2nd-person SINGULAR imperative, exactly the dual आ यातम् of rd028 with one fewer. Hold the two side by side: यातम् = "come, you two," याहि = "come, you one." The soma is described in a nominative string (सुताः … त्वायवः … पूतासः, "pressed … longing for you … purified"), strained अण्वीभिः, "through the fine filter" (instrumental of means). The dual you drilled all through RV 1.2 now has its singular foil.

sequence.sentence: नद्याः तीरे तिष्ठन् राजा दूरात् आगच्छन्तम् भ्रातरम् अपश्यत्। भ्राता श्रान्तः आसीत्। राज्ञा जलम् दातव्यम् इति मन्त्री अवदत्। राजा स्वयम् जलम् अददात्। पिता तत् पश्यन् अवदत् — एतत् एव राज्ञः कर्म, न अन्यत्। स्मरणीयम् एतत् सर्वैः।
sequence.translation: Standing on the bank of a river, the king saw his brother coming from afar. The brother was tired. The minister said that water was to be given by the king. The king himself gave water. The father, seeing that, said — "This alone is a king's work, not anything else. This is to be remembered by all."

sequence.vyakhya: तिष्ठन् आगच्छन्तम् पश्यन् — शतृ। दातव्यम् स्मरणीयम् — कृत्य। क्रिया अन्यथा अपि उच्यते।
sequence.vyakhya_en:
Six of the words here would be verbs in English and are not. तिष्ठन्,
आगच्छन्तम् and पश्यन् are participles; दातव्यम् and स्मरणीयम् are
gerundives. Only अपश्यत्, आसीत्, अवदत् and अददात् are finite.

राज्ञा जलम् दातव्यम् has no verb at all — an instrumental agent, a
nominative object, and a word meaning "to-be-given". Sanskrit says a great
deal this way, and it reads as ordinary statement once it stops being
turned into an English passive.

sequence.sentence: ग्रामे कुलालः वसन् घटान् अकरोत्। एकदा राज्ञः भ्राता तम् ग्रामम् आगच्छत्। कुलालम् कार्यम् कुर्वन्तम् दृष्ट्वा सः अवदत् — मम गृहे शतम् घटाः स्थापनीयाः। कुलालः अवदत् — कर्तव्यम् एतत्, किन्तु मूल्यम् दातव्यम्। भ्राता हसन् अवदत् — पिता मे राजा आसीत्, अहम् न मूल्यम् ददामि। कुलालः अवदत् — तर्हि घटाः न सन्ति। तत् श्रुत्वा भ्राता लज्जितः अभवत्।
sequence.translation: In a village a potter lived, making pots. One day the king's brother came to that village. Seeing the potter doing his work, he said — "A hundred pots are to be placed in my house." The potter said — "This is to be done, but the price is to be given." The brother, laughing, said — "My father was a king; I do not give a price." The potter said — "Then there are no pots." Having heard that, the brother was ashamed.
sequence.teaches:
a potter refuses a prince. Four participles and three gerundives against
six finite verbs; पिता and भ्राता carry their ऋ-stem grades through it.

sequence.vyakhya: कर्तव्यम् एतत्, किन्तु मूल्यम् दातव्यम्। द्वे कृत्ये, द्वौ पक्षौ।
sequence.vyakhya_en:
The potter's answer is two gerundives and nothing else: कर्तव्यम् एतत्,
किन्तु मूल्यम् दातव्यम्. He concedes the work and states his condition in
the same construction the prince used to give the order.

That is what makes it a refusal rather than a complaint. स्थापनीयाः was an
instruction; दातव्यम् answers it in kind.

sequence.sentence: शिष्यः वनम् अगच्छत्। तत्र सः फलानि अभक्षयत्, जलम् च अपिबत्। सायम् गुरुः अपृच्छत् — कुत्र आसीः। शिष्यः अवदत् — वने आसम्, गुरो। तत् श्रुत्वा गुरुः अवदत् — पठनम् एव तव कार्यम्, न तु वनगमनम्। शिष्यः अवदत् — क्षमस्व, अद्य प्रभृति पठेयम्। रामेण अपि तत् श्रुतम्, सः च अहसत्।
sequence.translation: The student went to the forest. There he ate fruits and drank water. In the evening the teacher asked — "Where were you?" The student said — "I was in the forest, teacher." Hearing that, the teacher said — "Studying alone is your work, not going to the forest." The student said — "Forgive me; from today I will study." Rāma too heard that, and he laughed.
sequence.teaches:
two action-nouns set against each other — पठनम् and वनगमनम् — and the
optative पठेयम् answering the teacher. अभक्षयत् and अपिबत् carry the
narrative; तच्छ्रुत्वा shows श्चुत्व at the join.

sequence.vyakhya: पठनम् वनगमनम् च — द्वे क्रियानाम्नी। एकम् कार्यम्, अन्यत् न।
sequence.vyakhya_en:
पठनम् and वनगमनम् are the same kind of word — an act named as a thing —
and the teacher sets one against the other. Sanskrit can compound the goal
straight into the noun: वनं गमनम् becomes वनगमनम्, going-to-the-forest, in
one word.

sequence.translation: Come, O Indra, urged on by the thought, hastened by the seers — up to the prayers of the soma-pressing worshipper.
sequence.teaches: आ याहि again in the singular, उप governing ब्रह्माणि "the prayers" as its goal, and धिया as the means

notes.en: instrument — "urged BY the thought" (the धी met in rd027)

notes.role: कर्तृकरणयोस्तृतीया → करण → धिया

notes.text: इषित = क्त-participle of इष् "impel" — "(you,) urged on"
padapāṭha splits विप्र-जूतः; विप्र "inspired seer" + जूत "sped, urged"

notes.text: सुतावत् = सुत "pressed soma" + मतुप् (वत्) "possessing"

sequence.vyakhya: इन्द्र — सम्बोधनम्; आ याहि — लोटि मध्यमपुरुषैकवचनम्; धिया — तृतीया करणे; इषितः विप्रजूतः — क्तान्तविशेषणे; उप ब्रह्माणि — द्वितीया कर्मणि गत्यर्थे; सुतावतः वाघतः — षष्ठी सम्बन्धे।
sequence.vyakhya_en: The same call — आ याहि, "come" — but now Indra is moved BY something and moves TO something. He is धिया इषितः, "urged on by the thought" (instrumental of means, the धी you met as धिया in rd027), and विप्रजूतः, "hastened by the seers." Where to? उप ब्रह्माणि वाघतः — "up to the prayers of the worshipper," where उप is a preverb steering the verb of motion onto an accusative goal (ब्रह्माणि), and वाघतः is a genitive ("of the worshipper"). Means in the instrumental, goal in the accusative, possession in the genitive — three cases you hold, in one line of the Veda.

sequence.translation: Come, O Indra, hastening, up to the prayers, O lord of the bay steeds; at the pressing take delight in us.
sequence.teaches: सुते "at the pressing" as a locative of occasion, the middle imperative दधिष्व "take, for yourself," and नः in the dative

sequence.vyakhya: इन्द्र हरिवः — सम्बोधनम्; आ याहि — लोटि मध्यमपुरुषैकवचनम्; उप ब्रह्माणि — द्वितीया गत्यर्थे; सुते — सप्तमी अधिकरणे; दधिष्व — लोटि आत्मनेपदम्; नः चनः — आत्मने ग्रहणम्। इन्द्रसूक्तत्रयं समाप्तम्।
sequence.vyakhya_en: The third and last call to Indra adds one new case: सुते, a LOCATIVE — "at the pressing," the occasion when the soma is pressed (अधिकरण, सप्तमी, by 2.3.36). The verb दधिष्व is √धा again — the root of दधाते "the two hold" in rd025 — but here a MIDDLE (आत्मनेपद) imperative, "take FOR YOURSELF," carrying delight (चनः, the noun of the very चनस्यतम् "take pleasure" that opened the hymn in rd026). The triplet to Indra is complete: three times "come," each adding a case — instrument, goal, and now occasion.

sequence.sentence: नगरे धनवान् वणिक् वसति स्म। सः चिन्तयत् — किम् मया कर्तव्यम्, केन मम जीवनम् सफलम् भवेत्। एकः मुनिः अवदत् — दानम् कुरु। तत् श्रुत्वा वणिक् दरिद्रेभ्यः अन्नम् अयच्छत्। तस्य दानेन बहवः जनाः अतुष्यन्। रामेण तत् दृष्टम्, सः च अवदत् — एतत् एव धर्मस्य आचरणम्।
sequence.translation: In a city there lived a wealthy merchant. He thought — "What should I do? By what would my life be fruitful?" A sage said — "Practise giving." Hearing that, the merchant gave food to the poor. By his giving many people were satisfied. Rāma saw that, and said — "This alone is the practice of dharma."
sequence.teaches:
दानम्, दानेन and आचरणम् name acts as things across one story. भवेत् asks
what would make a life fruitful; रामेण closes with णत्व across the ए.

sequence.vyakhya_en:
जीवनम्, दानम्, आचरणम् — three acts named as things, and the story turns on
treating them that way. A life can be fruitful, a giving can satisfy people,
a practice can be pointed at. None of them needs a verb.

sequence.translation: O helpers, upholders of men, O All-Gods, come — you bestowers, to the soma of the worshipper.
sequence.teaches: the address turns plural — after the dual Aśvins and Indra alone, the All-Gods as a crowd: विश्वे देवासः in the vocative plural, and आ गत "come, you all"

notes.text: ओमास् = Vedic nom./voc. pl. of ओमन् "helper, friend"

plural (contrast dual अश्विना rd026, singular इन्द्र rd029)

notes.en: "all" — qualifying देवासः, the standard epithet विश्वे देवाः "All-Gods"

notes.text: देवासः = Vedic voc./nom. pl. of देव (classical देवाः)

sequence.vyakhya: ओमासः चर्षणीधृतः विश्वे देवासः दाश्वांसः — सम्बोधनबहुवचनम्; आ गत — लोटि मध्यमपुरुषबहुवचनम्; दाशुषः — षष्ठी; सुतम् — द्वितीया कर्मणि।
sequence.vyakhya_en: The number completes its circle. RV 1.3 has now addressed a DUAL (the Aśvins, आ यातम्), a SINGULAR (Indra, आ याहि), and here a PLURAL — विश्वे देवासः, "all the gods," a whole company, bidden आ गत, "come, you all." Set the three imperatives of √गम्/√या side by side: यातम् (two), याहि (one), गत (many). Every vocative here is plural too — ओमासः, चर्षणीधृतः, दाश्वांसः. They come दाशुषः सुतम्, "to the worshipper's pressed soma" (genitive + accusative goal). One hymn has now drilled the entire तीन वचन.

sequence.sentence: अद्य दूतः नगरम् अगमत्। सः राज्ञः पुरतः अवादीत् — शत्रवः सेनाम् अनयन्, ग्रामान् च अदहन्। राजा तत् अश्रौषीत्, क्षणम् च तूष्णीम् आसीत्। ततः सः अवादीत् — यत् त्वया उक्तम् तत् सत्यम् चेत्, अहम् अद्य एव सेनाम् प्रेषयामि। मन्त्री अवदत् — देव, धैर्यम् एव बलम्। राजा अकार्षीत् यत् मन्त्री अवदत्।
sequence.translation: Today a messenger went to the city. He spoke before the king — "The enemies led out an army, and burned the villages." The king heard that, and was silent a moment. Then he spoke — "If what has been said by you is true, I send the army this very day." The minister said — "Your majesty, steadiness alone is strength." The king did what the minister said.

happened today. शत्रवः and राज्ञः show the visarga taking a sibilant and
a stop; तूष्णीम् holds its ष् unchanged.

sequence.vyakhya: अद्येति लुङः निमित्तम्। अगमत् अवादीत् अश्रौषीत् अकार्षीत् इति चत्वारः लुङः। अनयन् अदहन् अवदत् इति लङः, तयोः भेदः कालमात्रे। यत् त्वया उक्तम् इति भावे क्तम्, त्वयेति कर्तरि तृतीया। चेदिति न वाक्यादौ तिष्ठति।
sequence.vyakhya_en: अद्य sets the tense: four verbs here are aorists — अगमत्, अवादीत्, अश्रौषीत्, अकार्षीत् — and three are the ordinary past in लङ् — अनयन्, अदहन्, अवदत्. The two sit side by side in one paragraph, so the difference is a matter of what the sentence is doing rather than of what happened. अश्रौषीत् shows the ष् of सिच् after वृद्धि, while तूष्णीम् carries a ष् that no join produced. यत् त्वया उक्तम् puts the agent in the instrumental and the verb in a participle — the clause has no finite verb at all, and तत् सत्यम् answers it with none either.

sequence.vyakhya: विश्वे देवासः अप्तुरः तूर्णयः — सम्बोधनबहुवचनम्; सुतम् आ गन्त — द्वितीया गत्यर्थे लोटि बहुवचनम्; उस्राः इव स्वसराणि — उपमा (इव), द्वितीया गत्यर्थे।
sequence.vyakhya_en: The plural call repeats — सुतम् आ गन्त, "come to the soma, all of you" — but the verse closes with a SIMILE: उस्राः इव स्वसराणि, "like cattle (coming) to their pastures." इव "like" marks the comparison; उस्राः ("cattle") is the standard (nominative), and स्वसराणि ("pastures") is its accusative goal, mirroring सुतम्, the gods' own goal. The grammar of the simile is the grammar of the main clause — a goal-of-motion accusative in both halves. As cattle to the fold, so the gods to the soma.

sequence.sentence: द्वौ भ्रातरौ क्षेत्रम् अभजेताम्। ज्येष्ठः अवादीत् — अद्य अहम् अर्धम् अगृह्णाम्, त्वम् च अर्धम् गृहाण। कनिष्ठः तत् अश्रौषीत्, किन्तु न अतुष्यत्। सः ग्रामस्य वृद्धान् अपृच्छत् — केन एषा भूमिः विभक्ता। वृद्धाः अवादिषुः — यः स्वयम् विभजति सः न स्वयम् गृह्णाति। तत् श्रुत्वा ज्येष्ठः लज्जितः अभूत्, कनिष्ठाय च वरम् अर्धम् अददात्।
sequence.translation: Two brothers divided a field. The elder spoke — "Today I have taken half; you take the other half." The younger heard that, but was not satisfied. He asked the village elders — "By whom was this land divided?" The elders spoke — "He who divides himself does not himself take." Hearing that, the elder became ashamed, and gave the better half to the younger.
sequence.teaches:

both numbers. विभक्ता names the act as done; वृद्धाः and अवादिषुः close on
visarga at the pause.

sequence.vyakhya: लुङः चत्वारि रूपाणि — अवादीत् अश्रौषीत् इति प्रथमपुरुषे एकवचनम्, अवादिषुः इति बहुवचनम्, अभूत् इति भू-धातोः अपुसीयम्। ज्येष्ठः कनिष्ठः इति इष्ठन्प्रत्ययान्तौ। केन एषा भूमिः विभक्ता इति कर्मणि क्तम्, कर्तरि तृतीया।
sequence.vyakhya_en: The aorist widens here: अवादीत् and अश्रौषीत् are third singular, अवादिषुः is third plural of the same verb as अवादीत्, and अभूत् is √भू with no सिच् at all — the ending sits straight on the root. ज्येष्ठः and कनिष्ठः are the same suffix इष्ठन् on two opposed adjectives, and they carry the whole plot between them. केन एषा भूमिः विभक्ता asks the question with a participle and an instrumental agent, and the elders answer with a present-tense generality rather than a fact about this field.

sequence.vyakhya: विश्वे देवासः अस्रिधः एहिमायासः अद्रुहः वह्नयः — प्रथमाबहुवचने कर्तृविशेषणानि; मेधम् — द्वितीया कर्मणि; जुषन्त — प्रथमपुरुषबहुवचनम्। विश्वेदेवसूक्तत्रयं समाप्तम्।
sequence.vyakhya_en: The hymn's grammar turns one last time: from ADDRESS to STATEMENT. Through rd032–033 the gods were vocatives ("O All-Gods, come!"); here देवासः is NOMINATIVE — the SUBJECT — qualified by a string of nominative adjectives (अस्रिधः "unfailing," एहिमायासः a bahuvrīhi "whose power approaches," अद्रुहः "guileless," वह्नयः "bearers"). The verb is no longer an imperative TO them but a 3rd-person wish ABOUT them: मेधं जुषन्त, "may they enjoy the offering." The same noun in two cases across one triplet — vocative when called, nominative when described — is the whole lesson of address vs predication. The Viśvedevas triplet, and three-quarters of RV 1.3, complete.

sequence.vyakhya: पावका सरस्वती वाजिनीवती धियावसुः — प्रथमैकवचने स्त्रीलिङ्गकर्तृविशेषणानि; वाजेभिः — तृतीया; यज्ञम् — द्वितीया कर्मणि; वष्टु — लोटि प्रथमपुरुषैकवचनम्।
sequence.vyakhya_en: The last triplet of the hymn turns to a single FEMININE deity: सरस्वती, an ई-stem noun of the same नदी class you first declined in rd010. She is the subject (nominative), wrapped in feminine epithets — पावका ("purifying," with the टाप् feminine-आ of 4.1.4), वाजिनीवती ("rich in abundance"), धियावसुः ("treasure of thought"). The verb वष्टु is a 3rd-person SINGULAR imperative — "may she desire" — a wish made ABOUT her, not a command TO her. After the dual, singular-Indra, and plural triplets, the hymn closes on one goddess, in the feminine.

sequence.sentence: अद्य राजा सभाम् अगमत्। तत्र दूतः अवादीत् — शत्रवः पराजिताः, ग्रामाः च रक्षिताः। राजा तत् अश्रौषीत्, मन्त्रिणः च अपृच्छत् — केन एतत् कृतम्। मन्त्रिणः अवादिषुः — यः स्वयम् न भाषते सः एव अकार्षीत्। ततः राजा तम् वीरम् आह्वयत्, वरम् च अददात्। सः वीरः तूष्णीम् आसीत्, न च किञ्चित् अयाचत।
sequence.translation: Today the king went to the assembly. There a messenger spoke — "The enemies are defeated, and the villages protected." The king heard that, and asked the ministers — "By whom was this done?" The ministers spoke — "He who does not speak of himself is the very one who did it." Then the king summoned that hero, and gave a boon. That hero was silent, and asked for nothing.
sequence.teaches:
अगमत्, अवादीत्, अश्रौषीत्, अवादिषुः, अकार्षीत् — five aorists in one
scene. पराजिताः and रक्षिताः stand as predicates without a verb.

sequence.vyakhya: पञ्च लुङः एकस्मिन् प्रसङ्गे — अगमत् अवादीत् अश्रौषीत् अवादिषुः अकार्षीत्। पराजिताः रक्षिताः कृतम् इति कर्मणि क्तानि, तिङन्तम् अन्तरेण। मन्त्रिणः इति द्वितीयाबहुवचने प्रथमाबहुवचने च समानम्।
sequence.vyakhya_en: Five aorists carry the scene, and three of the sentences have no finite verb at all — शत्रवः पराजिताः, ग्रामाः रक्षिताः, केन एतत् कृतम् all rest on a participle. मन्त्रिणः appears twice, first as the accusative of the persons asked and then as the nominative of the persons answering; nothing in the form distinguishes them, only the verb each one stands beside. The hero's silence is the point of the last sentence and also its grammar — तूष्णीम् आसीत् and न किञ्चित् अयाचत say it twice, once with an indeclinable and once with a verb.

sequence.sentence: चो॒द॒यि॒त्री सू॒नृता॑नां॒ चेतं॑ती सुमती॒नां। य॒ज्ञं द॑धे॒ सर॑स्वती॥
sequence.translation: Impeller of true sayings, awakener of right thoughts — Sarasvatī has upheld the sacrifice.
sequence.teaches: two feminine agent-nouns governing the genitive — चोदयित्री … सूनृतानाम्, "impeller of true words" — and the perfect दधे "she has upheld"

notes.text: चोदयित्री = feminine agent-noun (तृच् → तृ + ई) of चुद् "impel" — "the urger"

notes.en: feminine agent-noun in apposition to सरस्वती (nominative)
genitive governed by the agent-noun — "impeller OF true words"

notes.role: षष्ठी शेषे → सूनृतानाम्

notes.text: चेतन्ती = feminine present participle (शतृ + ई) of चित् "perceive" — "awakening"

notes.en: feminine participle in apposition to सरस्वती

words.gloss: of right thoughts, of good intentions

notes.text: padapāṭha splits सु-मतीनाम्; सु "good" + मति "thought"

notes.en: genitive governed by the participle — "awakener OF good thoughts"

notes.role: षष्ठी शेषे → सुमतीनाम्
कर्मणि द्वितीया → यज्ञम्

words.gloss: she has upheld, she has established

notes.en: "hold, establish" — the √धा of दधाते (rd025) and दधिष्व (rd031), here PERFECT
3rd person singular — perfect middle "she has held"

sequence.vyakhya: चोदयित्री चेतन्ती सरस्वती — प्रथमैकवचने स्त्रीलिङ्गकर्तृविशेषणानि; सूनृतानां सुमतीनाम् — षष्ठी कर्तृकर्मसम्बन्धे; यज्ञम् — द्वितीया कर्मणि; दधे — लिटि प्रथमपुरुषैकवचनम्।
sequence.vyakhya_en: Sarasvatī is named by two feminine agent-words: चोदयित्री ("the impeller," a तृच्-agent-noun made feminine with ई) and चेतन्ती ("awakening," a present participle, शतृ + ई). Both GOVERN a genitive — चोदयित्री सूनृतानाम् "impeller OF true words," चेतन्ती सुमतीनाम् "awakener OF good thoughts" — the षष्ठी शेषे relation (2.3.50). Her act is दधे, "she has upheld," a PERFECT of √धा, the same root you have now seen as a present dual (दधाते, rd025), a middle imperative (दधिष्व, rd031), and now a perfect. One root, four tenses-and-moods, across the Saṃhitā.

source.ref: RV 1.3.12 (whole ṛc; saṃhitā + padapāṭha) — closes RV 1.3
source.curated: complete verse, taken whole; twelfth and final ṛc of RV 1.3. Accent verbatim from sri-aurobindo.co.in

sequence.sentence: म॒हो अर्णः॒ सर॑स्वती॒ प्र चे॑तयति के॒तुना॑। धियो॒ विश्वा॒ वि रा॑जति॥
sequence.translation: Sarasvatī makes the great flood known by her banner; she illumines all our thoughts.
sequence.teaches: two preverb+verb pairs (प्र चेतयति "makes known," वि राजति "shines over") + the instrument केतुना ("by her banner") — closing the whole hymn

notes.role: कर्मणि द्वितीया → अर्णः

words.gloss: by her banner, by her light-of-intelligence

notes.en: instrument — "BY her banner (she makes it known)"

notes.role: कर्तृकरणयोस्तृतीया → करण → केतुना

notes.en: object — what she illumines (the धी "thought" of rd027, now plural object)

notes.role: कर्मणि द्वितीया → धियः (acc. pl.)

notes.en: preverb — "apart, over," with राजति → "shines over, illumines"

sequence.vyakhya: महः अर्णः सरस्वती प्र चेतयति केतुना — द्वितीया कर्मणि, तृतीया करणे, प्रथमपुरुषैकवचनम्; धियः विश्वाः वि राजति — द्वितीयाबहुवचनं कर्मणि। ऋग्वेदस्य तृतीयं सूक्तं समाप्तम्।
sequence.vyakhya_en: The hymn closes with two preverb-verbs that mirror each other: प्र चेतयति, "she makes (it) forth-known," and वि राजति, "she shines over." Each preverb steers the sense of the verb. She makes known महः अर्णः, "the great flood" (accusative), केतुना, "by her banner" (instrument); she illumines धियः विश्वाः, "all the thoughts" (accusative plural) — the धी "thought" you have met since rd014, now the very thing the goddess of insight lights up. Object in the accusative, means in the instrumental, agent in the nominative: the कारक machinery of the whole reader, in the Veda's own words. **RV 1.3 is complete** — three hymns of the Ṛgveda (1.1, 1.2, 1.3) now read end to end.
